podcast.title: Cotton Club Debut (1938)
podcast.body: She began performing at the Cotton Club in 1938, initially on a two-week trial engagement for $500 a week. Her performances there involved a parody of church services, with dancers acting as "holy rollers," mocking her religion while her music remained devoted to it. "She started playing the Cotton Club in 1938."

podcast.title: Manchester 1964 Performance
podcast.body: In 1964, Tharp was filmed for the "Wigrenard the TV" blues TV program at the abandoned World War Hymn Road railway station in Manchester, performing alongside other black American music greats like Muddy Waters. By this time, she was primarily known as a blues musician, despite her consistent style, due to music evolving and re-categorizing her. "There's fascinating footage of her, in 1964, film Wigrenard the TV, playing at the abandoned World War Hymn Road railway station in Manchester."

podcast.title: "Godmother of Rock and Roll"
podcast.body: Her profound and intense influence on foundational rock and roll figures such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis, and Jerry Lee Lewis earned her the prestigious title of "Godmother of Rock and Roll." This recognition highlights her crucial role in shaping the nascent genre. "And her influence was so intense and so profound on people like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis and Jerry Lee Lewis that she has been called the Godmother of Rock and Roll."

podcast.title: Accolades and Honors
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe is a member of both the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Blues Hall of Fame, and was honored with her own US postage stamp, recognizing her immense contributions to music. "Sister Rosetta Tharp from 1944 and a member of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the Blues Hall of Fame and a woman who had her own US-posted stamp."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Sam Price
podcast.body: Tharp's collaboration with pianist Sam Price was musically significant but personally strained. Price initially disliked her open tuning and non-jazz key playing, insisting on a capo, and also combining gospel with boogie-woogie. He was eventually persuaded by Tharp's intimidating mother, and despite the success of their hit "Strange Things Happening Every Day," he resented only receiving a flat fee. "Sam Price did not get along with Tharp."

podcast.title: Declining Popularity in US, Rise in Europe
podcast.body: Her popularity in the US waned in the 1950s, but she maintained a strong following in Europe. "Rosetta Tharp's popularity started to wane in the 1950s, at least in her home country, but she retained her following in Europe."

podcast.title: First Stadium Rock and Roll Guitarist
podcast.body: Tharp is considered the first person to play rock and roll guitar in stadiums. This notable event was her third wedding, which took place at Griffith Stadium (home of the Washington Senators), drawing 20,000 attendees for her marriage ceremony and subsequent gospel show, featuring fireworks shaped like her playing guitar. She signed the wedding contract seven months before finding a husband. "She is probably the first person to ever play rock and roll guitar in stadiums, and not only that, she played rock and roll guitar in a stadium, at her wedding, her third wedding to be precise, which took place at Griffith Stadium, the home of the Washington Senators and the homestead 20,000 people came to see her get married and perform a gospel show afterwards."

podcast.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe achieved immense success as a gospel singer in the 1930s and 1940s, later venturing into soul and R&B. Her profound influence on artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis, and Jerry Lee Lewis earned her the title "Godmother of Rock and Roll." "And her influence was so intense and so profound on people like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Elvis and Jerry Lee Lewis that she has been called the Godmother of Rock and Roll."

podcast.title: Godmother of Rock and Roll
podcast.body: She is considered by some to be the "godmother of rock and roll" due to her significant contributions and influence across multiple genres. "if somebody deserves to be called the godmother of rock and roll, it's her, Sister Rosetta Tharp."

podcast.title: Gospel Music Innovator
podcast.body: Tharp made modern and cutting-edge music in the 1930s and 40s, which, despite John Hammond's view, would prove far more important than most swing bands. She was distinct from other gospel performers like Thomas Dorsey and Mahalia Jackson, as she traveled extensively for revival meetings rather than staying in one city. "Sister Rosetta Tharp was one of the great singers of her generation, and one of the great guitar players of all time, and she was making music that was as modern and cutting edge as anything else made in the 1930s and 40s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Gospel Success and Crossover Appeal
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp achieved significant success as a gospel singer throughout the 1930s and 1940s, later expanding her sound into soul and R&B, showcasing her versatile musical talent. Her ability to blend sacred and secular styles contributed to her wide appeal and lasting influence. "She became monstrously successful as a gospel singer in the 30s and 40s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Hidden Figures

podcast.title: Influence on Jerry and the Pacemakers
podcast.body: Her version of "This Train" significantly influenced later artists, including Jerry and the Pacemakers, a major Mercybeat band, who recorded their own version of "My Babe" months after Tharp's UK performances, demonstrating an unexpected connection between gospel and their sound. "Indeed, only a few months after Rosetta Tharp's UK performances, Jerry and the Pacemakers, one of the biggest bands of the new Mercybeat sound, who'd had three number one records that year in the UK, were recording their own version of My Babe."

podcast.title: Media Attention
podcast.body: Her performances at the Cotton Club garnered significant attention, with Time Magazine featuring her and remarking on her ability to "swing" the same songs in both church and nightclub settings. "Time Magazine even did a feature on her, and how she swings same songs in church and nightclub."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Partnership with Marie Knight
podcast.body: Her partnership with fellow gospel singer Marie Knight was highly successful, creating a unique gospel sound. Their relationship was an "open secret" within the gospel music community, which was more tolerant of homosexuality/bisexuality. Knight, however, denied the relationship throughout her life, likely due to her conservative church devotion and career dependence on it. They stopped working together in 1950, but Knight handled Tharp's funeral in 1973. "Her partnership with Marie Knight may have been a partnership in more than one sense."

podcast.title: Pioneer of Electric Guitar Distortion
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp was one of the very first musicians to intentionally use distortion on the electric guitar, a technique that would later become fundamental to rock music. Her innovative approach to the instrument had a significant impact on guitarists like Eric Clapton and Keith Richards. "There's more to she was one of the very first people to use distortion on the electric guitar."

srcs.episode: Hidden Figures

podcast.title: Pioneer of Rock and Roll Guitar
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp is credited as being as responsible as anyone for the style of rock and roll, particularly its focus on the guitar, and essentially invented the guitar style later adapted by blues legends like T-Bone Walker and B.B. King. "But one black woman is as responsible as anyone for the style of rock and roll, and in particular for its focus on the guitar."

podcast.title: Pioneering Black Queer Woman
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp was a queer black woman active in the 1940s, whose music spanned and influenced blues, jazz, gospel, and early rock genres. "She was a queer black woman in the 1940s who burned through blues, jazz, gospel, and early rock."

podcast.title: Pioneering Gospel-Rock Fusion
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp began combining electric guitar and gospel music in the 1930s and 1940s, a practice that later influenced artists like Elvis, Ray Charles, and Johnny Cash. She is recognized for establishing the idea of blending religious themes with popular music genres. "The idea of melding religion and popular music, well the likes of Elvis, Ray Charles, Johnny Cash, they just continued on with what she started."

podcast.title: Portrayal at Spirituals to Swing Concerts
podcast.body: At John Hammond's 1938 Spirituals to Swing concerts, despite her innovative style, Tharp was portrayed as less sophisticated than big band music on the same bill, primarily because she was performing religious music. "but portrayed her as somehow less sophisticated than the big band music on the same bill."

podcast.title: Posthumous Recognition
podcast.body: Sister Rosetta Tharp died in 1973 and received overdue recognition when she was inducted into the Rock Hall of Fame in "last year" (from the perspective of the podcast recording). "Rosetta Tharp died in 1973 and never really got the recognition she deserved."

podcast.title: Quitting Lucky Millinder's Band
podcast.body: She eventually quit Lucky Millinder's band without notice because she was increasingly pressured to sing secular numbers, like "Tall Skinny Papa," which made her uncomfortable, despite enjoying the band and making lifelong friends like Dizzy Gillespie. "So eventually she quit the millinda band without giving notice and went back to performing entirely solo, at least at first."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Taking Gospel to Sinners
podcast.body: After her first marriage ended, Tharp moved to New York and began playing in nightclubs and theaters for secular audiences, performing gospel music that encouraged dancing and excitement, a departure from Mahalia Jackson's approach of playing church music for church people. "Rosetta Tharp was taking the gospel to the sinners."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Touring in Segregated America
podcast.body: Tharp and Knight (and later Tharp solo) toured in their own bus driven by a white man. This offered crucial advantages in the deeply segregated US, allowing them access to public places, acquire takeout food from white-only restaurants, and have accommodation on the bus when no hotels would serve black people, leveraging a sexual double standard that made a black woman with a white man (assumed to be sleeping together) acceptable. "This gave them a number of advantages in a deeply segregated and racist country."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 5: "This Train" by Sister Rosetta Tharpe

podcast.title: Transition to Electric Guitar
podcast.body: While with Lucky Millinder's band, Tharp switched from acoustic to electric guitar, which revolutionized her playing style. The electric guitar's sustain allowed her to play single-note lead lines, relying on the orchestra for chordal pads, contrasting with her earlier need to constantly play new notes on acoustic guitar. "She'd also switched to playing an electric guitar rather than an acoustic, and the effect on her guitar playing was extraordinary."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Profound Influence on Blues and Rock Pioneers
xref.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe had a deep impact on the trajectory of the blues and on the pioneers of rock and roll, including major figures like Little Richard, Chuck Berry, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Johnny Cash, all of whom were ardent fans. Her work also captivated British musicians such as Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck. "What is not in dispute is that sister Rosetta Tharp had a profound effect on the course of the blues, and then with the pioneers of rock."
